subject: Pathology
summary: Left‑sided heart failure is a failure of the left ventricle to pump blood efficiently, causing pulmonary congestion and reduced systemic output. It is most often due to ischemic heart disease or hypertension.

sections.p: Left‑sided heart failure occurs when the left ventricle cannot eject blood adequately, leading to increased pulmonary venous pressure and pulmonary congestion. Diagnosis combines clinical signs, imaging, and biomarkers.

t.b: Is the patient experiencing heart failure? High levels (>125 pg/mL) suggest HF, especially when symptoms are present.
Is the left ventricle pumping efficiently? EF <40% confirms systolic HF; 40‑49% indicates mid‑range HF.
Does the lung show congestion? Kerley B lines, interstitial edema, or pleural effusion support HF.

sections.p: The New York Heart Association (NYHA) classifies functional limitation, while the ACC/AHA stages (A–D) describe disease progression and prognosis.
b: ACC/AHA A–D: risk, symptoms, structural changes

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the top causes are ischemic heart disease, hypertension, rheumatic valve disease, and infectious myocarditis.
b: Ischemic heart disease (MI, coronary artery disease)

sections.p: Patients report dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Physical exam shows tachycardia, S3 gallop, and pulmonary crackles.
Use tests that answer specific questions; if unavailable, rely on clinical judgment and basic labs.

t.b: Is the patient in heart failure? High levels support diagnosis.
What is LV function? EF, wall motion, valve disease.
Does the lung show congestion? Edema, pleural effusion.
Are there renal dysfunction or electrolyte disturbances that affect treatment?

sections.p: Rapidly worsening dyspnea, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmias, and renal failure are urgent complications.
Treat the underlying cause, then support circulation and relieve congestion. Drug choice balances efficacy and safety in low‑resource settings.
b: ACE inhibitors or ARBs – reduce afterload, improve survival
Beta‑blockers – slow heart rate, improve EF
Spironolactone – RAAS blockade in advanced HF

t.b: Does the patient have hypertension or LV dysfunction? These drugs lower afterload and improve survival.
Is the patient fluid overloaded? Diuretics reduce pulmonary congestion.
Is the patient in sinus rhythm with LV dysfunction? They improve EF and reduce mortality.
Is the patient in NYHA III–IV? It adds mortality benefit but watch potassium.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of symptoms, weight, BP, and labs; lifestyle changes; vaccination; early treatment of infections.
Right‑sided HF, COPD exacerbation, pneumonia, and pulmonary embolism can mimic pulmonary congestion.
b: Right‑sided HF – peripheral edema, jugular venous distension

faq.q: What is the earliest symptom of left‑sided heart failure?
faq.a: Dyspnea on exertion appears before orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

faq.q: Why is an S3 gallop significant?
faq.a: It indicates increased filling pressures and is a marker of systolic dysfunction.
Yes, over‑diuresis can reduce renal perfusion; monitor creatinine and electrolytes.

exam: Explain how ischemic heart disease leads to left‑sided heart failure and describe the compensatory mechanisms.
List the diagnostic criteria for left‑sided heart failure using BNP, echocardiography, and chest X‑ray.
Outline the first‑line pharmacologic therapy for a patient with systolic left‑sided heart failure and explain why each drug is chosen.
